items.title: This Delhi Mom Beat Burnout By Growing Tiny Green Paradise In Her 98 Sq Ft Balcony
items.blurb: The clock had just touched 11 on a weekday morning when I called Dipalee Nitin Rahangdale. On the other side of the phone came the soft sound of water splashing against terracotta pots, followed by a warm voice asking me to wait for a moment. “I am just watering my plants. Can you give me a minute?” she asks gently. A few moments later, the rustling leaves settled into the background as she returned to the call from the balcony of her rented apartment in Delhi. At 32, she speaks with a calmness that comes from finding inner peace after emotionally exhausting years, and from learning to rebuild life slowly through nature and creative expression . Her balcony is not grand by any means. Measuring just 14 by 7 feet, it is small, compact, and tucked into a city apartment. Within this limited space, she has created something astonishing. Hanging vines spill gracefully from railings, philodendrons curl around shelves, money plants trail across corners, and nearly 50 plants stand healthy under her care. Every inch of the balcony carries intention, patience, and healing, making it feel alive beyond its greenery alone. "Gardening became therapy for me," she says softly. "People think peace comes from money, success, or other people. But emotionally, everyone needs something that belongs only to them. You need a hobby that heals you from within. For me, that became gardening." Today, thousands of people know her through her Instagram page, @WabiSabiWithDipalee , where she shares glimpses of slow living, indoor gardening, and mindful spaces. Her videos are comforting and easy to follow. There are no extravagant makeovers or luxury aesthetics designed purely for social media validation. Instead, her content reflects ordinary life in a simple, beautiful way. A woman watering plants in the morning sunlight. A mother preparing potting mix with her child. Peaceful reflections about mental health, patience, and finding beauty in imperfection. It is this honesty that has helped her build a loyal online community of over 4,069 followers who connect with the peaceful world she has created. Her journey feels even more touching because this little balcony garden has become a shared space between her and her six-year-old son, Kavish. While many parents struggle to pull children away from screens, he spends his afternoons helping his mother water plants, plant seeds, and rearrange pots. Sometimes, he leaves cartoons midway to sit beside her while she works with soil and leaves. Together, mother and son are growing something bigger than a garden. The corporate life that slowly drained her Before becoming a gardening content creator, Dipalee spent years working in the corporate sector while trying to balance marriage, motherhood, and constant work schedules. Like many women, she strongly valued financial independence and wanted to build her own identity through work. Every inch of the balcony carries intention, patience, and healing, making it feel alive beyond its greenery alone. "I always wanted my own identity and the ability to stand on my own feet, so being financially independent and earning for myself was always something that mattered to me," she says in a conversation with The Better India . But slowly, the pressure of corporate life began draining her emotionally. Her office hours officially stretched from 9.30 in the morning to 7 in the evening, but reality was far harsher. Meetings continued late into the night because senior management arrived towards the end of the day. By the time she returned home, it was nearly 9 pm, and whatever energy remained had already been consumed by exhaustion. "I could not spend time with my son," she recalls. "The whole day would disappear in work, and I used to come home feeling emotionally empty." In June 2023, after years of pushing herself through exhaustion, she made the difficult decision to quit her job, one that felt especially hard for someone who valued independence and self-identity . "Leaving work affects you mentally, especially as a woman, when there is a sense of guilt attached to stepping away from a career, but I came to realise that I needed peace, and I needed time for myself and my child," she says. Her elder sister, Rupali Ravindra Rahangdale, watched this emotional transition closely from Pune. According to her, the difference between the Dipalee of a few years ago and the woman she is today is impossible to ignore. "She was constantly stressed because of work," she says. "I had seen her become mentally exhausted. But gardening changed her completely. It made her calmer, more positive, and much more patient." Throughout her difficult phases, Rupali became one of her strongest emotional support systems. "Whenever she felt demotivated with gardening, I would tell her not to stop and remind her that one day her hard work would pay off, so I shared her videos with people and kept motivating her constantly because I genuinely believed in what she was creating," she says warmly. The childhood memory hidden in marigold flowers Dipalee's connection with plants did not begin in adulthood. It had existed within her since childhood. Growing up in Maharashtra, she was surrounded by homes where gardening was simply a part of life. Her family maintained a kitchen garden like many households around them, but while others focused on vegetables, she found herself naturally drawn towards flowers and decoration. "We used to grow marigold flowers during Diwali," she says with a smile that instantly softens her voice. "I still remember decorating the house with those flowers. Those are some of my happiest childhood memories." Even as a child, she loved arranging spaces and decorating corners beautifully. While many children developed an interest in cooking or household work, she found joy in aesthetics and greenery. "I was never really drawn to cooking," she laughs, "but I have always loved flowers, home decor, and the process of turning spaces into something peaceful." As life became busier, however, gardening slowly disappeared into the background. After moving to Delhi and entering professional life, she barely had time for hobbies. The pace of adulthood consumed her attention completely. Yet somewhere within her, that childhood love for plants remained alive. Her journey feels even more touching because this little balcony garden has become a shared space between her and her six-year-old son, Kavish. Then came August 2019, a turning point she now looks back on with gratitude. After switching jobs and spending more time at home, she bought her very first plants . "I started with a money plant, aloe vera, and tulsi, just very easy-to-care-for plants that could survive without much effort," she recalls. At the time, she had no idea those three plants would eventually transform her entire life. The plants that died before the garden bloomed Like many beginners, she initially learnt gardening through YouTube videos and internet tutorials. But the process came with confusion, mistakes, and heartbreak. "A lot of my plants died in the beginning," she says honestly. "Sometimes because of wrong information online, and sometimes because I did not understand the plant properly." One of her biggest lessons came through jade plants. "Everyone used to say jade plants are indoor plants, even nursery owners would sell them that way, but when I observed them closely myself, I realised they actually need bright sunlight to survive," she explains. At another point, she followed online advice suggesting kitchen waste could be directly added into soil as fertiliser, but she later realised that only peels were actually helpful, while the rest led to fungus and pest attacks that damaged several plants. "I felt terrible," she admits. "There were times when I would almost cry after losing a plant." But slowly, gardening began to teach her lessons that went far beyond plant care, building her into someone more patient, observant, and emotionally strong, even in difficult moments. "Gardening taught me that every environment is different," she explains. "You cannot blindly follow someone else's advice. You need to understand your own home, your sunlight, your balcony, your weather." Over time, her tiny balcony grew into a flourishing indoor foliage garden filled with snake plants, spider plants, philodendrons, money plants, aloe vera, bougainvillea, jade plants, wandering jew plants, umbrella trees, adeniums, lilies, air plants, areca palms, tulsi, zig-zag cactus, and many more varieties. Because the balcony receives limited sunlight, she primarily focuses on foliage plants and low-maintenance greenery. Living in a rented apartment also influenced her gardening style significantly. "I did not have the option of a terrace garden, and moving heavy outdoor plants from one room to another is extremely difficult, especially with monkeys and birds outside that damage them, so indoor gardening became the best solution for me," she explains. Why did she name her page 'Wabi Sabi'? Her Instagram page name, @WabiSabiWithDipalee , reflects the philosophy she now follows consciously. Inspired by the Japanese concept of Wabi Sabi (finding beauty in imperfection), she believes beauty exists in imperfection, simplicity, and authenticity rather than polished perfection. "Social media makes people feel that everything has to look perfect, from homes to aesthetics to lives, but I believe real beauty actually exists in imperfect things too," she says. This philosophy is evident in the way she decorates her balcony . Instead of expensive decor, she reuses simple items creatively, proving that peaceful spaces do not require luxury. For Dipalee, gardening slowly turned into emotional healing. "When I sit with my plants, my stress disappears," she says calmly. "Gardening slows your mind down." Her routine remains intentionally simple. Every day, she spends around half an hour checking soil moisture, watering plants only when necessary, pruning leaves occasionally, and adding vermicompost whenever required. Instead of chemical pesticides, she uses turmeric to prevent fungal infections naturally. "The biggest mistake people make is overwatering," she explains with a laugh. "Plants usually die from too much care rather than too little." The little boy who leaves cartoons for plants But perhaps the most beautiful development has been the bond gardening created between her and Kavish. When Dipalee first became a mother, many people warned her that raising a child and maintaining plants together would be impossible. Even as a child, she loved arranging spaces and decorating corners beautifully. "People used to say that children would spoil plants and throw soil everywhere, but in my experience, my son and my plants grew together naturally, learning to coexist and care for each other over time," she says. Initially, her son occasionally played with soil while crawling around the balcony. But slowly, he began understanding that plants required care and gentleness. Today, at six years old, he actively participates in almost every gardening activity. "He helps me water plants, make potting mix, plant seeds, and repot plants," she says proudly. She believes gardening has changed him emotionally, too. Earlier, like many children, he spent long hours watching cartoons. Now, whenever she works on the balcony, he leaves the television behind and runs towards her eagerly. "He has become more caring," she says. "If he sees a plant somewhere, he immediately asks if we can bring it home." More importantly, gardening has taught him patience and acceptance. "When you plant seeds, they do not grow overnight, so he is learning to be patient, to wait for things to mature slowly, and to understand that not every plant survives, which is also teaching him that failure is a natural part of life," she explains. Sometimes, his innocent dreams leave her emotional. "He tells me that when he grows up, we will open a seed shop together," she says, laughing softly. Growing slowly, but authentically In April 2025, Dipalee finally decided to share her journey online through Instagram. Unlike creators chasing overnight virality, she focused entirely on authenticity. "My audience is growing slowly, but organically," she says. "I want genuine people connecting with me." Today, her content revolves around indoor gardening, balcony decor, mindful living, and emotional well-being through nature. Her videos capture small, personal moments from daily life: rearranging foliage in the morning sunlight, preparing potting mix with Kavish, or discussing mental peace and self-growth. In the future, she hopes to convert her passion into something larger. "I would love to help people create peaceful balcony spaces," she says. "I want to teach them which plants suit different homes and how gardening can improve mental health." And if she ever gets her dream home, she already knows exactly what she wants. "I want either a penthouse or a ground-floor home with lots of gardening space," she says instantly. As our conversation ended, she returned to watering her plants while Kavish hovered nearby excitedly, asking questions about a new sapling they had recently brought home. Watching them together, it became evident that this little balcony was never only about gardening. Every day, she spends around half an hour checking soil moisture, and watering plants only when necessary. It was about healing slowly after burnout. About slowing down in a world obsessed with speed . About finding emotional peace through nature. And perhaps most importantly, it was about understanding that even the smallest rented spaces can bloom beautifully when nurtured with patience and love. items.title: Unable to Farm After an Accident, 91-YO 'Amma' Grew 3000 Trees Beside Her Kerala Home
items.blurb: For years, Devaki Amma’s days began in the paddy fields of Muthukulam, a coastal village in Kerala’s Alappuzha district. Farming was the rhythm of her life, work she had known since childhood and continued alongside her husband, Gopalakrishna Pillai, a retired headmaster. Then, at 46, a car accident brought that rhythm to a sudden stop. The injury severely restricted her movement, and doctors advised her to avoid physical strain for nearly three years. For someone used to working outdoors from dawn, the long stretch of enforced rest felt unbearable. The fields she had tended for decades were suddenly beyond her reach. Life, as she knew it, had changed overnight. How recovery turned into a habit of planting Confined largely to her home, Devaki Amma began planting a single sapling on the sandy plot near her house, land that had until then only been used for post-harvest activities . It gave her something to do while her body healed. She planted another, then another. There was no plan to build a forest. It was simply a way to pass the days without her usual work. That small, repeated act did not stop once she recovered. Friends and relatives began bringing seeds and cuttings on their visits, and her husband and children joined in the effort. Instead of chemical fertilisers, Devaki Amma relied on leaf litter, mulching and manure from home-reared cattle to steadily improve nutrient-poor coastal sandy soil. Photograph: (AI-Generated image) Her daughter Thankamani, who would go on to head the Environmental Engineering department at a Thiruvananthapuram College, grew up watching this quiet, steady labour. What had started as a way to escape boredom slowly turned into a shared family project, and then into Devaki Amma's life's purpose. Turning sandy land into a living forest Over more than four decades, Devaki Amma's saplings spread across nearly five acres of coastal sandy soil, a stretch of land she named Thapovanam. She worked without formal training, relying instead on close observation of the soil and the local climate . Mulching, organic manure from home-reared cattle, and careful retention of leaf litter gradually improved land that was never expected to hold a forest. As Kerala's monsoon pattern shifted over the decades, with longer dry spells followed by concentrated bursts of heavy rain, Devaki Amma adjusted her methods rather than abandoning them. Her family adapted their mulching techniques at intervals to prevent waterlogging and protect root systems, a set of solutions drawn entirely from years of trial and repeated observation rather than any textbook. Long before receiving the Padma Shri, Devaki Amma's conservation work earned the Indira Priyadarshini Vrikshamitra Award in 2003 and the Nari Shakti Puraskar in 2018. Photograph: ( The Better India ) Two ponds within Thapovanam have never run dry. They support groundwater recharge, help prevent seawater from seeping into the coastal soil, and sustain aquatic life through the year. The forest also holds an Indian bael tree estimated to be around 200 years old, far older than Thapovanam itself, now standing within an ecosystem that grew up around it. 3000 trees in Kerala’s forest-less district Alappuzha is the only district in Kerala without natural forest cover , which makes Thapovanam more remarkable. The forest today holds over 3,000 recorded trees, plants, shrubs and creepers, including rare and medicinal species increasingly hard to find elsewhere in the state. It shelters peacocks, owls, the emerald dove and migratory birds, alongside butterflies and other small wildlife, functioning as a repository for native Kerala plant species under threat from habitat loss. Everything is maintained organically, without chemical fertilisers, using methods Devaki Amma developed over decades of trial and observation. She built all of this without institutional funding or a trained team, working largely without public recognition for most of those four decades. Her methods now draw interest from a newer generation of tree planters, including Krishnakumar S , who has helped build over 40 dense urban forests to cool Indian cities. From one sapling to a Padma Shri Devaki Amma, now 91, is widely known across Kerala as ‘Vanamuthassi’, or grandmother of forests. Her work drew national attention well before this year, including the Indira Priyadarshini Vrikshamitra Award in 2003 and the Nari Shakti Puraskar in 2018, and a mention by former President Ram Nath Kovind in his Republic Day address. This year, she received the Padma Shri, India's fourth-highest civilian honour, in the Unsung Heroes category. and was the only recipient from Kerala. Thapovanam is now visited by students, researchers and nature enthusiasts studying grassroots biodiversity conservation, and Devaki Amma has encouraged schools, colleges and households across the state to grow native and medicinal plants of their own, often providing seeds and seedlings herself. Her daughter Thankamani now cares for her full time, while the rest of the family continues to help maintain the forest. Devaki Amma still tends her plants daily, urging everyone she meets to plant at least one tree. Her four decades of quiet, repeated effort stand as proof of what patience, a family's support and a single sapling can eventually become. items.title: International Tiger Day: 7 Extraordinary Habitats That Prove Tigers Can Thrive Almost Anywhere
items.blurb: Most of us picture tigers prowling through dense tropical jungles. But the world's largest cat has mastered landscapes far more diverse than popular imagination allows, from icy forests in Russia to tidal mangrove swamps in India, and from towering Himalayan foothills to Southeast Asia's rainforests. On International Tiger Day, here's a journey through the remarkable homes that continue to shelter one of Earth's most iconic predators. A tiger silently padding through waist-high grass. Another weaving through tangled mangrove roots as tides rise around it. Yet another leaving fresh paw prints on snow in temperatures that plunge below -30°C. They all belong to the same species. For centuries, tigers have evolved into masters of adaptation, surviving in landscapes so dramatically different that they seem like homes for entirely different animals. While many people imagine them living exclusively in dense jungles, the tiger's range stretches across some of the planet's most extraordinary ecosystems . These habitats aren't just beautiful — they are among the most biologically rich and ecologically important landscapes on Earth. They also reveal another important fact: saving tigers means protecting an astonishing diversity of ecosystems. 1. The frozen forests of Russia Perhaps the last place anyone expects to find a tiger is in snow. Yet the Amur (Siberian) tiger, the world's largest tiger subspecies, inhabits the coniferous and mixed forests of Russia's Far East, with a small population extending into northeastern China. Winter temperatures here routinely fall below -30°C, and snowfall blankets the forests for months. The Siberian tiger was also called "Amur tiger", "Manchurian tiger", "Korean tiger", and "Ussurian tiger", depending on the region where individuals were observed. Photograph: (Appaloosa/Wikipedia) Unlike their tropical cousins, these tigers have thick fur, larger paws that act like natural snowshoes, and an extra layer of body fat to survive the bitter cold. Their lighter orange coats blend surprisingly well with snowy landscapes broken by tree trunks and winter shadows. It is the northernmost home of any wild tiger on Earth. 2. India's mangrove kingdom Now imagine the exact opposite. Instead of snow, there are shifting tides. Instead of dry forest trails, there are muddy islands crisscrossed by tidal creeks. The Sundarbans, spanning India and Bangladesh, is the world's largest mangrove forest and home to one of the planet's most unique tiger populations. Tigers of world’s largest mangrove forest, Sundarbans Tiger Reserve. pic.twitter.com/ad99AcYKNj — Trikansh Sharma (@trikansh_sharma) April 27, 2026 Here, Bengal tigers have adapted to life among salt-tolerant trees, tidal channels, and muddy terrain. They are exceptional swimmers. As sea levels rise because of climate change, the Sundarbans is also becoming one of the most vulnerable tiger habitats on Earth . 3. The endless grasslands Not all forests are dense. Some tiger landscapes are wide, open grasslands stretching as far as the eye can see. In reserves like Kaziranga, Manas, and Dudhwa, tall elephant grass grows over four metres high, creating natural cover for predators. These floodplain ecosystems are incredibly productive, supporting dense populations of deer, wild pigs, and buffalo, the prey that sustain healthy tiger populations. This tiger was born to sparkle ✨ This Golden Tiger of Kaziranga is worth more than solid gold… VC:In the clip pic.twitter.com/rP0Wc3RRUL — Susanta Nanda IFS (Retd) (@susantananda3) January 30, 2024 The annual floods that replenish these grasslands also maintain one of India's richest wildlife landscapes, shared by rhinos, elephants, swamp deer, and hundreds of bird species. 4. The Himalayan foothills The forests below the Himalayas present yet another world. Protected landscapes such as Corbett, Rajaji, and parts of Bhutan and Nepal combine river valleys, rocky hills, sal forests, and mountain streams. Tigers here navigate steep terrain that demands strength, agility and endurance. Jim Corbett National Park houses a thriving population of over 260 Bengal tigers, boasting one of the highest tiger densities among Indian national parks. Photograph: (Sriroopa Dutta) As temperatures rise globally, scientists believe these higher-elevation forests could become increasingly important for tiger conservation. 5. Southeast Asia's tropical rainforests The rainforests of Thailand, Malaysia, Myanmar, and Indonesia represent some of the oldest forests on Earth. Dense vegetation, towering trees, and year-round rainfall make them challenging places for both predators and researchers. Tigers living here often have enormous territories because prey densities are lower than in India's grasslands. These forests are biodiversity hotspots, sheltering clouded leopards, sun bears, hornbills, tapirs and countless other species alongside tigers. 6. Dry deciduous forests India's best-known tiger reserves, such as Bandhavgarh, Kanha, Pench, Ranthambore, and Tadoba, lie within dry deciduous forests. Unlike evergreen jungles, these forests change dramatically with the seasons. Leaves fall during summer, creating open woodlands where prey animals become easier to spot. During the monsoon, the forests transform into lush green landscapes teeming with life. A playful cub puts its skills to the test, trying out a stalking trick picked up from its mother. What may look like a game today is actually an important learning phase, helping young tigers understand the wild around them. Every crouch, stalk and surprise. pic.twitter.com/gglIyS9G7K — Pench Tiger Reserve (@PenchMP) June 21, 2026 These habitats support some of the world's highest tiger densities, proving that seasonal forests can be just as important as tropical rainforests. 7. Swamps, wetlands, and riverine forests Many tiger habitats revolve around water. Across India, Nepal and Southeast Asia, riverine forests and wetlands provide year-round prey, dense vegetation and reliable freshwater. These ecosystems also help regulate floods, recharge groundwater, and support millions of people downstream. Protecting tigers here often means safeguarding rivers that sustain both wildlife and human communities. Tiger is an “umbrella species” A tiger is often called an umbrella species, and protecting it means protecting everything beneath that umbrella. Each landscape that shelters tigers also stores carbon, purifies water, supports pollinators and sustains thousands of other plants and animals. The snow forests of Russia regulate northern ecosystems. The Sundarbans buffer devastating cyclones. India's grasslands support endangered rhinos and elephants. Rainforests absorb vast amounts of carbon while harbouring irreplaceable biodiversity. Saving these habitats, therefore, means protecting far more than a single charismatic predator. International Tiger Day is often celebrated with numbers: how many tigers remain, how many reserves exist, how populations have recovered. But perhaps the greatest conservation story lies in the astonishing places it still calls home. The tiger reminds us that resilience is written into nature's most extraordinary landscapes. Protecting the tiger, therefore, is about ensuring that these remarkable worlds, so different from one another, yet equally vital, continue to thrive for generations to come. items.title: One Photographer Got Children to Capture the Side of Chennai's 'Rowdy Area' the World Never Sees
items.blurb: When 20-year-old Rasiya Banu first picked up a DSLR camera, she was terrified. Growing up in Vyasarpadi, a working-class neighbourhood in North Chennai, she had become accustomed to hearing outsiders describe her locality with words like “dangerous”, “dirty”, or “rowdy area”. The labels followed her into classrooms and colleges. They shaped how others saw her before they knew her name. Today, Rasiya uses photography to challenge those assumptions. Through her lens, she documents football players, flood survivors, sanitation workers, grieving families , and the everyday lives of women in her neighbourhood. Each image becomes an act of reclaiming a story that others have long told on behalf of her community. Rather than chasing dramatic moments, documentary photographers often find the most powerful stories in ordinary routines that reveal resilience, dignity and everyday life. “People here are not as others describe. They are not criminals, and this place is not dirty,” she says, as she recalls her photography journey. Rasiya is one among several young photographers mentored by Chennai-based documentary photographer M Palanikumar through Vyasai Thozhargal, a grassroots collective in Vyasarpadi that works with children and first-generation learners. Over the past few years, the initiative has evolved beyond education support into something more ambitious: helping young people discover the power of visual storytelling and use it to represent their own realities. In a neighbourhood often reduced to headlines and stereotypes, cameras have become tools of confidence, creativity, and social change. A locality that refuses to be defined by stigma To understand why photography matters so deeply here, one must first understand Vyasarpadi. Vyasarpadi's community exhibition replaced gallery walls with neighbourhood streets, turning the very place often judged by outsiders into an open-air exhibition space. For decades, North Chennai neighbourhoods such as Vyasarpadi have been portrayed through a narrow lens. Popular culture frequently associates the area with crime, violence, poverty, or social unrest. Residents have repeatedly spoken about the discrimination they face simply because of their address. “Try taking a taxi to Vyasarpadi,” Palanikumar says. “Most drivers will refuse to come inside.” Yet the reality is far more complex. Behind the stereotypes are communities built on resilience, solidarity, labour, and aspiration. Families work long hours to support children's education . Women run households under difficult circumstances. Young people dream of becoming journalists, engineers, lawyers, artists, and teachers. Many of these stories rarely make it into mainstream narratives. That gap is precisely what Vyasai Thozhargal seeks to address. Documentary photography has long been used as a tool for social change, but participatory photography goes one step further by placing the camera in the hands of the community itself. Founded in 2014 by first-generation graduates from the locality, the collective began as an educational movement focused on ensuring that children from the neighbourhood remained in school. One of its most visible initiatives is Dr Ambedkar Pagutharivu Padasalai, a free tuition centre that today supports around 150 students. The organisation emerged from a simple belief: education can become a pathway to dignity and equality. Over time, however, its members realised that access to education alone was not enough. Children also needed spaces to express themselves, develop confidence, and see possibilities beyond what society expected of them. Photography became one such space. Handing over the camera Palanikumar is no stranger to using photography as a tool for social justice. Known for documenting marginalised communities and labour issues , he has long believed that those living a story are often best positioned to tell it. “If people from a particular community tell the story, the depth and emotions attached to that are even deeper,” he says. “The way they narrate their stories itself is a political statement.” With support from Vyasai Thozhargal, he began training young residents of Vyasarpadi in photography and visual storytelling. The programme was not structured like a conventional photography class. Community-led exhibitions shift the relationship between artist and audience by inviting visitors into neighbourhoods instead of isolating art inside galleries. Instead of directing students on what to shoot, he encouraged them to observe their surroundings, speak to people, and photograph what mattered to them. Participants were given access to cameras and taught technical skills, but equal importance was placed on empathy, observation, and storytelling. For many, it was the first time anyone had asked them to document their own lives. The transformation was remarkable. Over the course of more than a year, students produced thousands of photographs capturing neighbourhood celebrations, household labour, local traditions, friendships, environmental challenges, sports, and family life. What emerged was not merely a collection of images but an archive of lived experiences. The stories outsiders never see One of the most powerful examples came from Rasiya. Following the death of football player Priya, whose passing sparked widespread outrage across Tamil Nadu, Rasiya felt compelled to document the young athlete's story. “Priya was a stranger to me,” she says. “Yet I couldn't accept that her passing was reduced to a mere news headline.” Research consistently shows that when communities create their own visual archives, they challenge stereotypes far more effectively than narratives produced by outsiders. Through photographs and conversations with family members, she created a visual narrative that restored humanity to a story many had encountered only through breaking news updates. Other participants focused on equally intimate subjects. There were images of single mothers working tirelessly to support their families. Photographs of sanitation workers taking a brief tea break after long shifts. Portraits of elderly temple workers carrying out decades of service despite financial hardship. Some students documented flooding and climate impacts in North Chennai. Others explored gender, sports, friendship, and childhood. What connected all the projects was authenticity. Rather than searching for dramatic scenes, the photographers turned their attention to ordinary moments that revealed extraordinary resilience. “The students' outlook on life, spaces, and the people they engage with is vastly different from external projections,” Palanikumar observed. Their work challenged the tendency to view marginalised communities only through the lens of suffering. Instead, the photographs showed complexity: joy alongside hardship, aspiration alongside struggle, dignity alongside deprivation. When confidence begins to grow The impact of the initiative extends well beyond photography. For many participants, the experience has altered how they see themselves. Dr Ambedkar Pagutharivu Padasalai, run by Vyasai Thozhargal, now supports around 150 children with free educational assistance alongside creative learning opportunities. Young people who once hesitated to speak in public now discuss their work with visitors and journalists. Students who had never considered creative careers are exploring opportunities in journalism, media, and visual communication. Nandhini, one of the participants, is pursuing journalism. Others have spoken about wanting to continue documenting social issues affecting their communities. Photography has also created new forms of representation. Historically, communities such as Vyasarpadi have often been photographed by outsiders. The resulting images, while sometimes well intentioned, can still reinforce unequal power dynamics. Here, the photographers belong to the neighbourhood. They know the people they photograph. They understand the context behind every image. As Palanikumar noted, the students often notice details that outsiders might overlook. Their perspective is not observational. It is lived. An exhibition on the streets Perhaps the most symbolic expression of the initiative came through the exhibition Engal Therukkal Engal Kadhaigal, or Our Streets, Our Stories. Rather than displaying photographs inside a conventional gallery, organisers transformed the streets of Vyasarpadi into an exhibition space. North Chennai has produced celebrated sportspersons, musicians and artists, yet mainstream portrayals of the region have often focused disproportionately on crime and poverty. Hundreds of photographs were displayed outside homes and along neighbourhood lanes. Visitors walked through the community while viewing stories created by its residents. The choice was deliberate. “There is a need for actual recognition of North Chennai,” Palanikumar explained. “Every photo frame was placed outside their homes so that the exhibition attendees could easily communicate with them.” The exhibition challenged not only perceptions of Vyasarpadi but also assumptions about who gets to be an artist, whose stories deserve visibility, and where art belongs. For local residents, seeing their lives represented with dignity was deeply meaningful. For visitors, it offered an opportunity to encounter a side of North Chennai rarely portrayed in mainstream narratives. More than photography At its heart, the Vyasai Thozhargal initiative is not really about cameras. It is about access to creativity, self-expression and confidence. For children growing up in communities where opportunities are often limited, these experiences can be transformative. A camera can become a bridge between observation and action. Between invisibility and recognition. Community-led photography creates historical records that future generations can inherit, preserving neighbourhood memories that rarely appear in official archives. The young photographers of Vyasarpadi are proving that stories do not need to come from outside experts or visiting journalists. Sometimes, the most powerful stories emerge when communities are trusted to tell their own. As one message from the participating students declared before their exhibition: “What you've seen, heard, known and what you've told us. This isn't Vyasarpadi. Only we can share our stories. And now, we are doing so.” In neighbourhoods long spoken about by others, that simple act of self-representation may be the most powerful change of all.
